Debt repayment, visualized: the payment, the timeline and the interest

Compare repayment paths, inspect principal and interest, and see how the rate and monthly payment change a debt-free date.

The central idea

A payment decision changes both the time in debt and the interest paid. Check that the payment reduces principal before relying on a payoff date.

01

Follow the remaining balance

The first chart compares your selected monthly payment with the same payment plus an extra amount. The interest rate and starting balance stay fixed. The final payment is reduced to the amount owed rather than collecting a full payment after the debt is cleared.

At the start of the default example, CAD 10,000 at an assumed nominal annual rate of 18% incurs CAD 150 of interest over one simplified month. A CAD 300 payment therefore reduces principal by CAD 150 in that first month. Later interest falls as the balance declines.

The chart is not a reconstruction of a credit-card statement. Actual products may use daily accrual, different transaction rates, grace periods, fees and changing minimum payments. Read the agreement and statement before treating any modeled date as a contractual payoff quote.

02

Separate the amount borrowed from the financing cost

The stacked bars divide a completed repayment schedule into original principal and cumulative interest. Both paths repay the same starting principal. Any reduction in total paid comes from a change in financing cost under the selected assumptions.

Do not compare only the monthly payment. A lower payment can make the current budget easier while extending the repayment period and increasing interest. Conversely, a larger payment needs to be affordable; a plan that repeatedly forces new borrowing may fail to deliver the modeled saving.

If the selected payment is no larger than the first month’s interest, it does not reduce principal in this simplified model. The tool reports “Not repaid” instead of inventing a payoff date. It also withholds a lifetime-interest total when the schedule is not completed within the model limit.

03

Read the rate-and-payment matrix

The matrix uses your starting balance with a fixed set of rates and payments. Each cell shows months to repay, including a partial final payment. NR means the debt is not repaid within the 600-month limit, including cases where the payment fails to reduce the balance.

This is a sensitivity map. A lower rate is not assumed to be available, and a larger payment is not assumed to fit your budget. If a refinancing offer exists, compare fees, term, variable-rate risk and any collateral implications separately.

A rate cut and an extra payment affect the model through different channels. The former reduces the charge on the outstanding balance; the latter reduces the balance more quickly. A genuine comparison needs both the repayment schedule and the total cost.

04

Place the debt inside the whole budget

Make a list of all obligations, interest rates, due dates and minimum payments. The Government of Canada’s Six Steps to Get Out of Debt discusses directing extra repayment toward high-rate debt and, alternatively, small balances for motivation, while maintaining required payments.

The chart models one balance and cannot decide the entire order of repayment. Arrears, essential living costs, secured obligations, promotional terms and restrictions may change priorities. It also does not value employer matching contributions, tax effects or access to emergency cash.

Keep the avoided borrowing cost distinct from a risky investment’s expected return. Repaying a fixed-rate balance changes an interest obligation under its terms; an investment forecast does not guarantee that it will outperform that cost.

05

Check the recurrence and the implementation

The monthly recurrence is new balance = old balance × (1 + annual nominal rate ÷ 12) − actual payment, with payment capped at the amount owed. No new purchases or fees are added. A completed schedule satisfies total payments approximately equal to principal plus modeled interest, subject to rounding.

  1. Use the statement’s actual rate and identify any separate balances.
  2. Keep required payments current.
  3. Choose an extra payment that leaves a workable cash-flow margin.
  4. Confirm any prepayment restrictions or charges.
  5. Reconcile the next statement with the planned progress.

If the plan cannot cover essential costs and required payments, that is a cash-flow problem to address directly. A longer chart does not create the capacity to pay.
